The first thing we recorded was the drawer that held the spoons. My mother pulled it open, waited for my signal, and pushed it shut. Through the headphones I heard a quick silver commotion followed by a wooden knock. It was a fair recording of a drawer and a terrible recording of breakfast. At breakfast nobody waited for a signal. Somebody was usually standing in the way, buttering toast over the cutlery, and the person who wanted a spoon had to reach around that somebody with the particular tenderness or irritation the morning deserved.

“Do you want me to get in your way?” my mother asked.

We were selling the house. She had lived there forty-three years, I had lived there eighteen, and my brother Daniel claimed twenty, counting two summers when he kept his belongings in the garage but slept almost exclusively at his girlfriend’s. Our father had died in February. By July my mother had chosen a flat near the railway station, with a lift and a balcony just deep enough for two chairs, provided the people in them had no immediate plans to stand up. She had measured both chairs. The measurements, unlike most assurances offered to her since February, had made her feel better.

The recordings were my idea. I worked editing radio documentaries and had spent much of my adult life asking strangers to repeat things they had said more beautifully by accident. I knew enough to regret this habit and not enough to stop. I had brought a portable recorder, two microphones, a stand, several cables, and a pair of headphones with a repaired headband. My mother had expected something smaller. When I set it all out on the table she took the good tablecloth off first, as though I were about to clean a fish.

“What are we recording next?”

“The stairs,” I said.

“They’re not going anywhere.”

“Neither is the drawer.”

“Well,” she said, “you’ve got me there.”

On the stairs the fourth tread clicked at the left edge, the seventh gave a long complaint, and the little square landing made no sound at all. As children we had believed we knew a silent route upstairs. Listening to Daniel demonstrate it that afternoon, I discovered that the route would have deceived only a very generous audience. He planted one foot against the skirting board, swung the other over the seventh tread, grabbed the banister, and arrived at the landing breathing like a man bringing a wardrobe up behind him.

“Dad always knew,” my mother called from the kitchen. “He just didn’t fancy coming out to discuss it.”

Daniel played the recording back twice. The first time he laughed at the breathing. The second time he took the headphones off before the end and asked whether I had anything of Dad. I said I was sure I did. There were birthday videos, messages, a cassette from a holiday in Wales. What he meant, it turned out, was whether I had Dad saying Daniel’s name. On the birthday videos Dad usually held the camera. His messages began with “Hello, it’s me,” and ended, rather formally, with “Your father.” Neither of us could remember what was on the Welsh cassette.

We put it on the list. The list had begun on the back of an envelope with six items: stairs, drawer, front gate, boiler, rain in the conservatory, and the kitchen clock being wound. By supper it occupied three sheets of paper. Daniel wanted the old letter box, which delivered the post in two movements, a slap and a squeal. My mother wanted the bathroom tap before the plumber came on Wednesday. It made a noise she disliked and wished to play for the plumber, who had already failed on two visits to hear it. Her contributions tended to have a practical advantage over ours.

The gate was a disappointment. In my memory it announced each visitor in advance, giving a child on the sitting-room carpet enough time to decide whether to run to the door or hide behind the sofa. In fact the gate had been replaced in 2009. Its successor opened with the soft, costly efficiency of a hotel wardrobe. I stood by the hedge holding a microphone while Daniel went in and out three times. A woman walking a terrier crossed the road to avoid us. At last my mother leaned out of the upstairs window and told us the old hinges were in a tobacco tin in the shed.

There is a sort of hope peculiar to people clearing out a house: the hope that the next container will explain the contents of the last one. The tobacco tin contained four hinges, none in pairs, a brass number six, the broken pink leg of a plastic animal, and a Canadian dime. We never found the animal or the tobacco. Daniel put the six in his pocket. He lived at number forty-two, but that seemed a mean point to raise. I kept the dime because it bore the year of my birth and because nobody else wanted it, two qualifications that have filled a good many cabinets.

That night I slept in my old room on a mattress whose hollows no longer corresponded to my body. The recorder lay on the floor beside me. Around two in the morning I heard a train from the goods line beyond the allotments. It had been the last sound I heard on hundreds of childhood nights, though I could not remember ever hearing its beginning. I would become aware of it already under way, a low iron rhythm traveling through the dark along with my thoughts. By the time I found the recorder and worked out which way it was facing, the train had passed.

Instead I caught a minute and forty seconds of my mother downstairs. Water ran. A cupboard closed. There was a faint scrape that might have been a chair moving back from the table. Then I heard her laugh. It was a short, unguarded laugh, not one I had heard much lately. In the morning I asked what had been funny. She had gone down for a glass of water and found Daniel’s imitation of a council notice propped against the bread bin: RESIDENTS ARE ADVISED THAT THE FRONT GATE IS CURRENTLY UNDERGOING AN EXTENSIVE PROGRAMME OF LISTENING. Underneath, in smaller letters: NO DISCERNIBLE IMPROVEMENT IS ANTICIPATED.

“Did you record me in my nightdress?” she asked.

“Only the sound.”

“Thank goodness. It’s a dreadful nightdress.”

I offered to erase it. She thought for a moment and said I might erase the water running, if that was possible, since she had left the tap on longer than necessary and did not like to set a bad example. The laugh could stay. I tell this because it was the first time any of us had considered that the house might contain sounds a person did not wish to keep. Until then we had treated the microphone as a net drawn through clear water. Now we had to decide which things to put back.

At work I could spend an afternoon removing a refrigerator from an interview. Not the refrigerator itself, of course, but its low continuous note beneath a woman’s account of leaving home at sixteen, or a retired surveyor’s description of a landslip. Cut the note too aggressively and the speaker began to sound weightless, an oracle transmitting from a tiled lavatory. Leave it in and listeners in their own kitchens might never notice. I generally left a little. A human voice ought to sound as though it comes from somewhere, even if the somewhere is an appliance in need of service.

On Tuesday we found the cassette in a biscuit tin marked PHOTOGRAPHS, under some photographs in an envelope marked GUARANTEES. We borrowed a player from Mr. Shah next door. He came with it, reasonably enough; Daniel had borrowed his stepladder in 1998 and had yet to return it. The cassette began with several seconds of wind, followed by my own high voice explaining that we were at the seaside. More wind confirmed this. Then Daniel, aged seven, gave the football results for a league in which all the teams were named after puddings. Rice had beaten Sponge away from home in what sounded like difficult conditions.

Our father came on about halfway through. He said, “If you put your thumb there, love, all you’ll get is your thumb.” This was plainly advice about the camera and not the tape recorder. There followed a stretch of beach noise so vivid that Mr. Shah looked down at the carpet when a dog shook itself. My mother sat with her elbows on her knees. Daniel’s face had assumed the careful vacancy it wore when he was trying not to influence a penalty kick on television. We listened to the side run out. Our father had said eleven words, depending on what you did with “you’ll.”

“Other side?” Mr. Shah suggested.

The other side contained a French lesson. A brisk woman wanted directions to the municipal swimming pool. A man offered directions of such complexity that she would have been better off taking a bath at the hotel. We listened for nearly a minute, reluctant to be the one who pressed stop. Then my mother repeated the woman’s last sentence in an excellent accent. All those years, she said, there had been another cassette, and all those years she had wondered why the course started at lesson nine. Mr. Shah took his player home. Daniel followed him with the stepladder.

On Wednesday the plumber heard the tap. It happened before I could set up, and by the time I had attached the microphone he had diagnosed a loose washer. He replaced it in four minutes and stayed for tea and a discussion of parking regulations. My mother crossed the tap off the list with satisfaction. I felt briefly cheated, as if he had painted over a small fresco. Then I went upstairs to wash my hands and enjoyed the smooth, quiet turn of the handle. There were advantages to the future which had not been adequately represented on our sheets of paper.

Rain was forecast for Thursday. I set a microphone in the conservatory, which was what we called the narrow enclosure my father had built against the kitchen wall. It held a washing rack, a dead radio, and a geranium of fabulous age and uncertain loyalties. The geranium flowered whenever my mother announced that she was getting rid of it. Its latest reprieve had come the previous week, when a single red head appeared above the packing boxes. Daniel had agreed to take it home. His girlfriend from the summers in the garage was now his wife, and had stipulated that no additional furniture accompany the plant.

The rain arrived at four. The first drops clicked separately overhead; then their intervals shortened until the whole roof spoke at once. I had forgotten how loud it got. My mother came in carrying tea, and Daniel brought the last three biscuits on a saucer. For a while we watched runoff collect at the low corner where our father had repeatedly intended to fit a gutter. Through the headphones the roof sounded magnificent, broad and intricate. Without them it sounded even better, because I could feel the table trembling faintly under my wrist. I took them off. Daniel offered me a biscuit. It was soft.

“You know what I’d like?” my mother said.

Neither of us heard her over the roof, so she had to say it again. She wanted a recording of us trying to remember the name of the man who used to deliver potatoes. Not the name itself. She knew the name. She wanted the conversation in which we tried to remember it, because at some point Daniel would be so sure of a wrong answer that he would offer money, and I would start listing unrelated men with vans, and she would get to sit back knowing something. We gave it a go. Within forty seconds Daniel had lost five pounds.

By Friday we had thirty-seven recordings. Some were excellent. In one, the kitchen clock ticked its way through the silence after my mother finished winding it, and the sound seemed almost visible, like the neat punctures a sewing machine leaves in paper. Others required their labels. Without the words “airing cupboard” I would have identified that file as somebody taking a thick jumper off in a hurry. I copied everything onto my computer and made folders. Daniel asked me to send him the Welsh tape, including the puddings. My mother asked for the potato conversation. Neither requested the gate.

We moved her on a clear Monday. At the new flat the lift doors made a small bowing motion before they closed, as if apologizing to passengers for what was bound to be a short and unremarkable journey. The balcony faced west. From the left-hand chair, provided you turned your head a little, you could see the station platforms and a strip of countryside beyond the car park. My mother sat there while Daniel and I argued about the bookcase. Eventually she told us to put it where she had asked in the first place. A train pulled out. You could not hear it through the glass.

Several months later she rang me at work. She wanted to know how to make a recording on her phone. I began explaining where the microphone was, but she had already located the application and wanted to know what the red circle meant. I said it meant record. She said a circle hardly conveyed that information to a person coming fresh to the subject. A square for stop she could understand: it had the look of something planted solidly in your way. While we were discussing the triangle, she recorded both of us for almost three minutes and sent the result to Daniel, who replied that it was good to hear adults getting to grips with shapes.

That evening she sent a second file. At first I could hear only a faint traffic wash. Then came a rattle, a pause, and three descending notes of astonishing sweetness. Across the road from her balcony, my mother explained in the accompanying message, a boy was learning to play the trumpet. Every evening he began with those three notes. After that things deteriorated considerably, but the beginning was lovely, and she had thought I might like it. I listened again. Just before the trumpet started, there was my mother setting down her cup and drawing the other chair a little closer, to rest her feet on it, I suppose. She had left the balcony door open.
